teaching_objective: After this lesson, the learner can identify the opening and closing tag pattern in an HTML element and correctly match elements to their opening/closing or self-closing tag format.
teaching_approach:
Reuse the blueprint/skeleton analogy but focus on the 'snap' mechanism: each element is like a labeled box that snaps open (opening tag) and snaps shut (closing tag) around its content. For self-closing tags, the box is sealed in one piece (like a sticker). Use visual side-by-side examples to contrast a paragraph element (

...

) with an empty image tag (). Stress the pattern 'opening tag + content + closing tag' and show what happens when the closing tag is missing (content 'leaks' onto the rest of the page).
key_points: An HTML element consists of an opening tag, optional content, and a closing tag — the opening tag starts with '<' and the closing tag has a slash '/' before the tag name.

Self-closing elements (like and
) have no content and are written in a single tag (e.g., ).
Tags must be properly nested — the closing tag must match the opening tag and close in reverse order of opening.
misconceptions:
Beginners may think the closing tag includes a forward slash at the end of the opening tag (e.g., '

') — clarify that a separate closing tag with a leading slash is required for non-void elements.
Some may forget the slash in the closing tag entirely, causing the browser to treat everything after as content — emphasize that the slash is what signals the end.
Learners might attempt to put content inside a self-closing tag (e.g., 'text') — clarify that void elements cannot have content and are always self-closing.

## Prior lesson briefs
### 00.0 — Welcome to HTML Fundamentals
- Objective: After this lesson, the learner can explain what HTML is and why it is used to structure web pages.
- Approach: Use the analogy of a house blueprint: HTML provides the structure and layout of a web page, just like a blueprint defines the rooms and walls of a house. Emphasize that HTML is not programming but a markup language — it's about describing content, not logic.
- Key points:
  - HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language for creating web pages.
  - HTML is a markup language, not a programming language — it uses tags to describe content.
  - This course will teach you how to read and write HTML so you can build your own web pages.

### 01.0 — What is HTML?
- Objective: After this lesson, the learner can identify the role of HTML as a markup language and distinguish it from a programming language.
- Approach: Reinforce the 'blueprint' analogy from the welcome lesson but zoom in: just as a blueprint uses symbols (not code) to show where walls and doors go, HTML uses tags (not logic or variables) to show where headings, paragraphs, and images go. Emphasize that 'markup' means adding labels to content so the browser knows how to display it.
- Key points:
  - HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language — it uses tags, not instructions, to describe content.
  - A markup language adds meaning to text (e.g., telling the browser 'this is a heading'), while a programming language gives the computer instructions to follow.
  - You can think of HTML as the 'skeleton' of a web page — it defines the structure, but not the behavior or styling.
- Misconceptions:
  - Beginners often think HTML is like Python or JavaScript — they look for 'if' or 'for' keywords. Clarify that HTML has no logic or variables.
  - Some learners believe every HTML element changes the look of text (like making it bold or colorful). Remind them HTML is about structure, not style — that's CSS's job.
  - The word 'markup' might be unfamiliar. Explicitly connect it to 'marking up' a document with a highlighter or sticky notes — you're simply labeling content.

### 01.1 — The HTML Document Structure
- Objective: After this lesson, the learner can identify the four main parts of an HTML document (doctype, <html>, <head>, <body>) and match each with its purpose.
- Approach: Use the 'house blueprint' analogy one more time but now zoom in on the blueprint's sections: the title block (doctype and head) tells you what project this is and its metadata (like the architect's notes), while the floor plan (body) shows the actual rooms. Emphasize that every HTML page follows this same skeleton — it's not optional, it's the rule.
- Key points:
  - Every HTML document starts with <!DOCTYPE html> and a root <html> element that wraps everything.
  - The <head> contains metadata (like the page title) that is not displayed on the page.
  - The <body> holds all visible content — headings, paragraphs, images, links.
- Misconceptions:
  - Beginners often put visible content inside <head> because they confuse 'head' with the top of the page. Clarify that <head> is for information about the page (title, links to stylesheets), not for what users see.
  - Some learners forget the root <html> element and write tags directly after the doctype — reinforce that ALL content and metadata must live inside <html>.
  - The <!DOCTYPE html> looks like a tag but isn't an HTML element — it's a declaration that tells the browser this is HTML5. Do not close it.
